title: Only by love
hookLine: hatred never ends by hatred, only by love; this is an old law (Dhammapada 5)

lines: HE SAID THAT. IN THAT TONE.
cards: He said that. In that tone. In front of everyone.
Hours later the scene is still running: once in the shower, once in the car, and each time the comeback gets sharper. By now the argument has lasted far longer in one head than it did in the room.
The other person has probably moved on to lunch. The Dhammapada, a collection of the Buddha's sayings, has this scene in its first chapter. It even gives the replay.

teach.h: HE ABUSED ME, HE BEAT ME…
teach.b: First, the replay. In Max Müller's old translation, verse three goes: "He abused me, he beat me, he defeated me, he robbed me." In those who harbor such thoughts, the verse says, hatred will never cease.
Verse four turns it round: in those who don't harbor them, hatred will cease. The verses aren't about the insult. They're about the sentence we keep saying to ourselves afterward.

Then verse five: "hatred does not cease by hatred at any time: hatred ceases by love." It reads like common sense, and it's hard to live. Hitting back can look like ending it; the verse says it keeps it going.
Third, the Pali says non-hatred. Müller chose the English word love. The Pali word is averena: by non-hatred, by the absence of enmity.
So the verse isn't asking you to feel warm toward the person who wronged you, not today anyway. It's asking you to stop adding fuel. Love, in this verse, can start as simply putting the replay down.
That's what the verse calls it. Not a clever tactic for winning, just how hatred works, the way fire works. Feed it, and it burns.
Stop feeding it, and it goes down.

how: Buddhists read and recite the Dhammapada's verses, and loving-kindness meditation is one practice used to soften resentment toward people who have caused harm.

o: by non-hatred: the absence of enmity that lets hatred end
by answering a wrong with an equal and fair reply
by forgiving at once and forgetting the wrong entirely

games.q: the Dhammapada's opening verses — tap the pairs.
p: he abused me, he beat me…
don't harbor them, and hatred ceases

s: the verses are mostly about the insult itself
they're about the thoughts we harbor afterward: he abused me, he robbed me.
the Pali word Müller translated love means non-hatred
averena: by non-hatred, by the absence of enmity.
the verse calls this a new teaching
it calls it an old rule.

games.q: someone wronged you, and the sentence keeps running: he abused me, he robbed me. what do verses three and four say ends the hatred?
o: replaying it until it makes sense
games.why: in those who harbor such thoughts hatred will never cease; in those who don't, it will.

practice: Bring to mind one small hostility, not the deepest wound: a sharp email, a neighbor, a relative's comment.

Hear its replay sentence once, the he said, she did, then let it trail off each time it starts, the way you'd stop feeding a fire. You don't need to forgive or feel warm; just don't add a log, and rest with the breath.

wordCard.voice: Averena, Pali for by non-hatred, the word behind the Dhammapada's old rule that hatred ceases only by its absence, not by more hatred. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali, written here in Devanagari: by non-hatred, the word Max Müller rendered 'by love' in Dhammapada 5.

carryVoice: Your line: stop feeding it. Hatred ceases by its absence, not by more of it. See you tomorrow.
